completeSourceDiscovery.boundaryContinuationRule: a move beginning in lookbehind remains owned by the predecessor chunk

candidates.speaker: Frank Turek
candidates.proposition: Theism better explains reality because reality includes immaterial features that materialist atheism cannot explain.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly introduces Frank Turek immediately before this opening statement, and the uninterrupted first-person presentation follows.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is the opening thesis directly answering the debate motion and establishing the comparative explanatory standard for all subsequent arguments.
candidates.contextSummary: After introductory remarks, Turek defines the competing positions and states that immaterial aspects of observed reality favor theism over atheism.

candidates.speaker: Frank Turek
candidates.proposition: The universe's beginning and fine-tuning are best explained by a timeless, immaterial, uncaused intelligent creator.
candidates.attributionBasis: The passage remains within Turek's uninterrupted opening statement and is framed as the first component of his announced argument.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The cosmological and fine-tuning case supplies a principal positive argument for a creator and derives core attributes of the theistic cause.
candidates.contextSummary: Turek argues from a cosmic beginning and precisely calibrated physical constants to design, then identifies the cause as outside space, time, and matter.

candidates.speaker: Frank Turek
candidates.proposition: Unguided materialism cannot justify trustworthy reason or free choice, whereas theism can ground rational thought.
candidates.attributionBasis: The same identified speaker explicitly introduces reason as the next element of his structured opening case and continues without interruption.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This argument challenges atheism's ability to justify the reasoning used to affirm atheism, making it a central worldview-level explanatory objection.
candidates.contextSummary: Turek invokes evolutionary doubt about cognition and argues that purely molecular minds merely react, undermining confidence in reasoning and atheism itself.

candidates.speaker: Frank Turek
candidates.proposition: The information encoded in DNA points to an intelligent mind because meaningful codes arise from intelligent sources rather than repetitive natural forces.
candidates.attributionBasis: Turek explicitly marks information as the next component of his opening framework, with no speaker transition before the argument concludes.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The information argument is one of the named pillars of his cumulative case and provides a distinct inference from biological coding to intelligence.
candidates.contextSummary: Using messages, software, and the information content of cells as analogies, Turek argues that DNA's ordered code requires an intelligent cause.

candidates.speaker: Frank Turek
candidates.proposition: Objective moral rights and wrongs require a standard beyond humanity, so atheism cannot justify objective morality or human rights.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly announces morality as the next part of his case, and the moderator-designated opening statement remains uninterrupted.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The moral argument is a principal independent pillar of the cumulative theistic case and directly contests atheism's grounding of moral obligation.
candidates.contextSummary: Turek uses atrocities, rights, tolerance, and moral comparisons to argue that without a transcendent standard all moral judgments reduce to opinion.

candidates.speaker: Frank Turek
candidates.proposition: The reality of objective evil supports rather than defeats God's existence because evil presupposes objective good and an external moral standard.
candidates.attributionBasis: Turek expressly transitions from morality to evil within the same uninterrupted opening statement and develops the argument in his own voice.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This move converts a major apparent objection to theism into affirmative support for God, materially strengthening the comparative case presented.
candidates.contextSummary: After adding free will and stable natural laws to his cumulative chart, Turek argues that recognizing injustice requires an objective standard of justice.

candidates.speaker: Frank Turek
candidates.proposition: Science depends on immaterial preconditions such as logic, causality, reason, free will, realism, orderly laws, and morality that theism explains better than atheism.
candidates.attributionBasis: The passage is explicitly introduced as the science component of Turek's structured case and occurs before any change of speaker.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The argument addresses science as a major claimed advantage of atheism and makes its necessary foundations part of the positive case for theism.
candidates.contextSummary: Turek maintains that empirical inquiry must assume several nonempirical realities and ethical norms, which he says materialist atheism cannot supply.

candidates.speaker: Frank Turek
candidates.proposition: Reasoning from the cosmos, rationality, information, and morality identifies an immaterial, powerful, intelligent, purposeful, morally perfect, personal creator.
candidates.attributionBasis: Turek remains the uninterrupted opening speaker and explicitly synthesizes the previously presented effects into attributes of their proposed cause.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This synthesis connects the separate arguments to the specific theistic explanation defended in the motion rather than merely to unexplained phenomena.
candidates.contextSummary: Turek infers divine attributes from the effects already discussed and identifies the resulting cause with the classical theistic creator and sustainer.

candidates.speaker: Frank Turek
candidates.proposition: Atheism cannot explain the immaterial foundations it uses in argument, while theism provides a unified explanation of those aspects of reality.
candidates.attributionBasis: This is the explicit conclusion of Turek's uninterrupted opening statement, which ends before applause and Silverman's response begins.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The conclusion directly states the comparative verdict on the motion and integrates the preceding arguments into one cumulative explanatory claim.
candidates.contextSummary: Turek concludes that atheistic argument relies on reason, science, morality, and evil despite lacking a foundation for them, whereas theism grounds them.

candidates.speaker: David Silverman
candidates.proposition: Theistic first-cause reasoning converts gaps in present knowledge into an unsupported divine explanation without solving the origin question.
candidates.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted opening turn is introduced as David Silverman's, and his self-identification near the turn's beginning confirms the attribution.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This challenges the principal theistic inference from cosmic origins and frames the con side's recurring objection that unexplained phenomena do not establish God.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Turek's earlier claim that the universe requires a timeless, immaterial first cause identified with God.

candidates.contextSummary: Silverman characterizes cosmological arguments as appeals to ignorance, argues that alternative invented causes fit the same inference, and says exempting God merely relocates the unanswered origin question.

candidates.speaker: David Silverman
candidates.proposition: The universe's overwhelmingly inhospitable composition and Earth's limited habitability count against purposeful design for human life.
candidates.attributionBasis: The material occurs continuously within Silverman's identified opening statement, with no moderator cue or speaker transition before the next argument.
candidates.loadBearingReason: It directly contests the design and fine-tuning strand of the pro case by offering observed cosmic and terrestrial conditions as contrary indications.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Turek's earlier appeal to cosmic order and fine-tuning as evidence of an intelligent designer.

candidates.contextSummary: Silverman contrasts the scale of stars, planets, dark matter, and dark energy with the small habitable portion of Earth, concluding that any design was poor and not centered on humanity.

candidates.speaker: David Silverman
candidates.proposition: Morality is socially determined and relative rather than an objective law whose existence requires a divine lawgiver.
candidates.attributionBasis: The argument remains inside Silverman's uninterrupted opening turn and follows his design discussion without any indication of a speaker change.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This denies the moral-law premise supporting one of the pro side's principal arguments and supplies a human-social account of moral judgment and responsibility.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Turek's earlier contention that objective moral obligations exist and are grounded in God's unchanging nature.

candidates.contextSummary: Silverman denies objective morality, uses conflicting claims of divine moral authority to illustrate disagreement, and locates responsibility for judgments and choices in human society.

candidates.speaker: David Silverman
candidates.proposition: Admitting ignorance about cosmic origins is more reasonable than asserting God because inquiry has produced no verified supernatural explanation.
candidates.attributionBasis: These rows are part of Silverman's identified opening statement, and the first-person discussion of his atheism coheres with his established speaker identity.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move states the con side's positive epistemic standard for explaining reality and contrasts revisable natural inquiry with an allegedly unsupported supernatural conclusion.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Turek's claim that natural reality is best explained by an immaterial supernatural cause rather than atheism.

candidates.contextSummary: Silverman argues that uncertainty before the Big Bang should be acknowledged, says physical inquiry explains observed structures without God, and presents atheism as a revisable conclusion responsive to verified data.

candidates.speaker: David Silverman
candidates.proposition: Established evolutionary and stellar history conflict with a literal Genesis sequence and undermine Christianity's creation and original-sin account.
candidates.attributionBasis: The claim is delivered during Silverman's continuous opening statement, with explicit references to the opposing presentation and no intervening speaker transition.
candidates.loadBearingReason: It uses natural-history claims to challenge the reliability of a major theistic tradition's account of human origins and its associated theological explanation of reality.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: The preceding theistic presentation and introductory claim that the Bible was written under divine authority.

candidates.contextSummary: Silverman treats evolution as established, argues that it displaces Eden and original sin, and contrasts Genesis's ordering of Earth and light with the stellar formation of carbon before planets.

candidates.speaker: Frank Turek
candidates.proposition: Recognizable informational patterns provide positive evidence of intelligence, so design inferences need not be arguments from ignorance.
candidates.attributionBasis: A moderator announces the rebuttal after Silverman's applause, and the new speaker explicitly names David while defending the previously presented theistic case.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This directly answers the con side's governing God-of-the-gaps objection and rehabilitates intelligent-cause reasoning through comparisons with independently recognizable artifacts and messages.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Silverman's characterization of cosmological and design arguments as merely inserting God wherever knowledge is incomplete.

candidates.contextSummary: Turek distinguishes inference from known signs of intelligence from inference based on ignorance, using deliberately formed geological faces, linguistic information, and authored text as analogies.

candidates.speaker: Frank Turek
candidates.proposition: Because nature began and is therefore an effect, its cause cannot be natural but must transcend space, time, and matter.
candidates.attributionBasis: The rows continue Turek's announced rebuttal without interruption and explicitly answer David's treatment of the universe's creation as a knowledge gap.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This supplies the pro side's core explanatory inference from a beginning of physical reality to a supernatural cause possessing the attributes assigned to God.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Silverman's claim that no one knows what preceded the Big Bang and that a divine first cause merely fills ignorance.

candidates.contextSummary: Turek invokes astronomical support for a cosmic beginning, argues that nature cannot cause itself, and infers a cause beyond physical nature rather than a future natural explanation.

candidates.speaker: Frank Turek
candidates.proposition: Apparent defects do not negate design because design quality depends on intended purposes and every physical design involves constraints and tradeoffs.
candidates.attributionBasis: This is a continuous segment of Turek's rebuttal, introduced as an answer to the poor-design point and followed by a distinct response about materialism.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The argument protects the design inference from the con side's claim that cosmic inhospitability disproves purpose, while distinguishing imperfect execution from absence of design.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Silverman's argument that the universe and Earth are too inhospitable and inefficient to have been designed for humans.

candidates.contextSummary: Turek argues that judgments of good or bad design require knowledge of intended use, illustrates unavoidable performance and portability tradeoffs, and adds that imperfection remains compatible with design.

candidates.speaker: Frank Turek
candidates.proposition: Materialist atheism undermines confidence in reasoning because thoughts become determined molecular reactions, including the thought that atheism is true.
candidates.attributionBasis: The argument remains within Turek's announced rebuttal and explicitly addresses Silverman's assertion that atheistic arguments have not been theistically refuted.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is the pro side's self-defeat objection to atheism and supports its broader claim that rational and scientific inquiry presuppose immaterial realities unavailable to materialism.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Silverman's claim that atheistic methods reliably explain reality and have never been defeated by a theistic argument.

candidates.contextSummary: Turek presents reductive materialism as making beliefs products of prior physical causes, then argues that this account erodes reasons to trust scientific conclusions or atheism itself.

candidates.speaker: David Silverman
candidates.proposition: Humanly observed order and improbable personal existence do not establish design because observers necessarily assess the universe from conditions permitting their existence.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly announces David's rebuttal immediately before these rows, and the new speaker's argument answers Turek's design presentation.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move supplies an observer-selection response to the pro side's design inference and reframes apparent order as compatible with a largely chaotic, inhospitable universe.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Turek's rebuttal claim that recognizable order and information are positive indications of purposeful intelligent design.

candidates.contextSummary: Silverman analogizes his own highly contingent conception to fine-tuning reasoning, then argues that the universe appears ordered or designed because observers exist within rare local concentrations of matter and energy.

candidates.speaker: David Silverman
candidates.proposition: Evolution proceeds through cumulative selection across immense spans of time, so a sudden random arrangement analogy misrepresents it.
candidates.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted rebuttal is delivered by Silverman during his response to Turek's earlier Cheerios analogy.
candidates.loadBearingReason: It directly contests the analogy used to make natural processes appear incapable of producing organized biological complexity.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Turek's Cheerios analogy portraying naturalistic development as a random spill suddenly forming an organized message.

candidates.contextSummary: Silverman distinguishes gradual evolutionary accumulation from an instantaneous explosion or random spill and substitutes repeated incremental retention over time.

candidates.speaker: David Silverman
candidates.proposition: Biblical approval of violence against infants undermines the claim that scripture supplies objective morality matching ordinary moral judgment.
candidates.attributionBasis: Silverman explicitly introduces Turek's objective-morality claim and answers it with a biblical counterexample.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move attacks a principal theistic explanation of moral knowledge by alleging conflict between scripture and shared moral judgment.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Turek's contention that objective morality exists and that torturing babies is self-evidently objectively wrong.

candidates.contextSummary: Silverman invokes a passage praising the destruction of infants and argues that the Bible can conflict with the moral intuition Turek treats as objective.

candidates.speaker: David Silverman
candidates.proposition: Morality is historically and socially relative, and accepting that fact places responsibility for moral choices on human decision-makers.
candidates.attributionBasis: Silverman develops the position continuously through the close of his speaking segment before the format transition.
candidates.loadBearingReason: It supplies atheism's affirmative account of morality and responsibility while challenging the practical value of purported divine objectivity.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Turek's argument that relativism cannot condemn atrocities and that objective moral duties require a transcendent standard.

candidates.contextSummary: Silverman accepts difficult consequences of moral disagreement, argues that religious certainty can displace personal responsibility, and illustrates the alleged harm through historical and contemporary examples.

candidates.speaker: David Silverman
candidates.proposition: Relative morality still permits individuals and societies to object, judge, and assume responsibility without appealing to an external sacred standard.
candidates.attributionBasis: Silverman directly answers Turek's cross-examination question in a clearly attributable alternating exchange.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The answer addresses the immediate internal-consistency challenge that moral relativism would eliminate meaningful moral objection or judgment.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Turek's challenge that Silverman cannot call an adoption decision immoral after denying objective morality.

candidates.contextSummary: Silverman clarifies that denying objective morality does not end moral choice or protest; people still make judgments independently of holy books.

candidates.speaker: David Silverman
candidates.proposition: An omnipotent, omniscient, and benevolent God should not require infants to suffer cancer, creating a direct problem of evil for Christianity.
candidates.attributionBasis: Silverman deliberately changes the cross-examination topic to evil and formulates the challenge in his own extended questioning.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The argument directly tests whether theism better explains severe apparently unnecessary suffering under its central claims about God's attributes.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Turek's claim that objective evil points to objective good and thereby supports the existence of God.

candidates.contextSummary: Silverman denies that invoking objective evil resolves the issue and asks why a God able to prevent every case knowingly permits childhood cancer.

candidates.speaker: David Silverman
candidates.proposition: Divine foreknowledge and deliberate placement of the forbidden tree make God responsible for the fall and its foreseeable consequences.
candidates.attributionBasis: Silverman presents the Garden of Eden scenario directly after Turek's free-will defense of the existence of evil.
candidates.loadBearingReason: It challenges the free-will defense by relocating causal and moral responsibility from human agents to an omniscient creator's prior decision.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Turek's defense that evil entered the world through human free choice and that freedom is necessary for love.

candidates.contextSummary: Silverman argues that God knew exactly what Adam would do and could have placed or omitted the tree differently, yet chose the foreknown outcome.

candidates.speaker: Frank Turek
candidates.proposition: Although a sinless free world is logically conceivable, it may not be achievable because free creatures might sin in every feasible world.
candidates.attributionBasis: Turek explicitly takes the floor to identify the assumption in Silverman's scenario and delivers the full response.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is the principal answer to the claim that God could simply create free agents while guaranteeing that no one ever sins.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Silverman's claim that God could locate or omit the forbidden tree so that Adam would not sin and suffering would not follow.

candidates.contextSummary: Turek distinguishes logical possibility from actual achievability with free creatures, then frames the resulting biblical story as redemption after freely chosen sin.

candidates.speaker: Frank Turek
candidates.proposition: Knowing a future action does not cause it, just as knowing a recorded game's result does not remove the players' freedom when they acted.
candidates.attributionBasis: Turek introduces and develops the recorded-football-game analogy in direct response to Silverman's foreknowledge objection.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The analogy supports the crucial distinction between divine foreknowledge and divine causation on which Turek's free-will defense depends.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Silverman's argument that perfect divine foreknowledge leaves Adam no choice and makes God responsible for the fall.

candidates.contextSummary: Turek compares God's knowledge to a viewer who already knows a recorded game's score but did not thereby cause the players' original decisions.

candidates.speaker: Frank Turek
candidates.proposition: Finite observers cannot establish that suffering is gratuitous because its good consequences may emerge later, through other choices, or in eternity.
candidates.attributionBasis: Turek explicitly turns back to Silverman's gratuitous-evil challenge and gives a sustained multi-part response.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move directly defends theism's explanatory adequacy against apparently pointless evil and connects suffering to limited human perspective and eternal justice.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Silverman's contention that childhood cancer and other suffering lack sufficient purpose and therefore make a benevolent God culpable.

candidates.contextSummary: Turek argues that humans cannot trace all causal consequences, uses ripple effects to illustrate unknown goods, and adds that divine justice extends beyond earthly life.

candidates.speaker: David Silverman
candidates.proposition: An omnipotent God could realize any later good without childhood cancer, so unknown future benefits do not reconcile suffering with benevolence.
candidates.attributionBasis: Silverman answers Turek's enumerated defense point by point and restates the challenge to omnipotence and benevolence.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The rebuttal targets the central skeptical-theist response and argues that divine power makes severe suffering unnecessary even if later goods exist.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Turek's claim that finite humans cannot know whether present evil produces greater goods later in time or eternity.

candidates.contextSummary: Silverman rejects appeals to human limitation and an afterlife, arguing that an all-powerful being could secure every proposed benefit without leukemia or comparable evil.

candidates.speaker: Frank Turek
candidates.proposition: God did not experience a temporal delay before humanity, and life's information indicates intelligence rather than natural emergence.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator directs the question to Turek, whose answer continues coherently until Silverman explicitly challenges it.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The answer directly defends theism against the apparent lateness of humanity and Christianity while invoking the earlier information argument and Christian redemption.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: The question that cosmic and biological chronology makes humanity and Christianity appear to have arisen naturally after an implausibly long divine delay.

candidates.contextSummary: During audience questions, Turek answers a chronology objection with divine timelessness, intelligence at life's basis, retroactive salvation, and a providential account of Christ's historical timing.

candidates.speaker: David Silverman
candidates.proposition: Turek evades the chronological problem, while Christianity revised its creation account after evidence established an ancient Earth.
candidates.attributionBasis: Silverman directly addresses Turek by describing what the preceding answer did, and Turek begins objecting immediately afterward.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The reply uses the age of Earth to challenge Christianity's explanatory reliability and portrays later interpretations as adaptations to contrary scientific discovery.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Turek's answer that divine timelessness, biological information, and salvation history resolve the long chronology preceding Christianity.

candidates.contextSummary: Silverman says the response avoided the question and argues that an originally short Christian chronology was replaced by long-creation interpretations only after contrary evidence emerged.

candidates.speaker: David Silverman
candidates.proposition: Atheism offers honesty rather than religious consolation and makes people responsible for testing claims and making their own moral choices.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly assigns the multipart question to Silverman, and the uninterrupted first-person answer precedes Turek's allotted response.
candidates.loadBearingReason: Silverman gives a direct positive account of what atheism contributes: epistemic honesty, empirical testing, rejection of false hope, and personal responsibility.
candidates.contextSummary: Asked what atheism offers and how it improves life, Silverman contrasts honest inquiry with promises of heaven and argues that owning choices and consequences improves conduct.

candidates.speaker: Frank Turek
candidates.proposition: Silverman's praise of honesty, justice, freedom, proof, and better choices presupposes objective standards that atheism cannot supply.
candidates.attributionBasis: Turek announces that he is responding to everything Silverman just said and systematically identifies terms from the preceding answer.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is Turek's core transcendental objection that atheistic argument and moral evaluation depend on objective truth and value unavailable within Silverman's worldview.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Silverman's claim that atheism offers honesty, evidence-based testing, freedom of choice, responsibility, and outcomes that are better in his judgment.

candidates.contextSummary: Turek argues that debate itself assumes truth beyond personal opinion and that Silverman's evaluative vocabulary imports standards that atheism does not ground.

candidates.speaker: Frank Turek
candidates.proposition: The design inference from biological information is falsifiable because natural production of specified complex messages would defeat the need for intelligence.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator asks Turek whether his assertions are falsifiable, and Turek answers in the first person until Silverman begins a contrary DNA claim.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move defends the information argument's scientific legitimacy by specifying a potential falsifier and appealing to observed limits of repetitive natural laws.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: The audience question challenging whether Turek's asserted evidence for theism can in principle be falsified.

candidates.contextSummary: Turek says discovery of natural forces that generate specified complex messages would falsify intelligent causation, but maintains that observed laws have not done so.

candidates.speaker: David Silverman
candidates.proposition: Human concern for suffering arises from evolved social empathy, a trait shared with other animals, rather than objective morality grounded in God.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator directs the suffering question to Silverman, and his answer consistently uses an evolutionary social account before Turek objects.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The answer supplies a naturalistic explanation for compassion and prosocial conduct, directly addressing the theistic claim that moral motivation requires divine grounding.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: The challenge that atheists cannot coherently seek relief of suffering without objective morality grounded in a just God.

candidates.contextSummary: Silverman explains empathy as an evolved feature of social animals and argues that humans help others because mutual welfare supports life in society.

candidates.speaker: David Silverman
candidates.proposition: Arguments inferring God from unexplained origins remain god-of-the-gaps reasoning because there is no evidential basis for a law-transcending deity.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator asks Silverman to distinguish deductive theistic arguments from gap arguments, and Silverman answers until Turek says to hang on.
candidates.loadBearingReason: Silverman directly attacks the legitimacy of the cosmological, moral, and teleological inferences by denying evidence for the extraordinary entity they posit.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: The question asking whether classical deductive arguments for God differ from fallacious appeals to a deity wherever knowledge has a gap.

candidates.contextSummary: Silverman says deduction requires an evidential basis, while the proposed timeless, spaceless, all-powerful being violates known physical regularities and lacks such support.

candidates.speaker: Frank Turek
candidates.proposition: Hell is just separation from God chosen through sin, because divine love does not force unwilling people into God's presence.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator assigns Turek the question about divine power and evil, and Turek develops the answer continuously until Silverman's next challenge.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move addresses evil, judgment, salvation, and divine love by linking hell to free choice and presenting Christ as an available pardon rather than coerced belief.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: The challenge that an all-powerful God should remove evil and that failure to do so conflicts with divine power and love.

candidates.contextSummary: Turek says God will quarantine evil, distinguishes sin from failure to believe, and uses rejected courtship as an analogy for love that permits separation.

candidates.speaker: Frank Turek
candidates.proposition: Theism best explains the cosmos, reason, information, morality, evil, and science, whereas atheism cannot ground the realities its arguments employ.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator introduces Turek's uninterrupted closing, and the first-person synthesis runs through his explicit conclusion and thanks.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This closing consolidates Turek's entire comparative case, argues that atheism borrows immaterial foundations it cannot explain, and expressly concludes for the motion.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Silverman's debate-wide objections to God, religion, Scripture, objective morality, biological design, and theistic explanations of reality.

candidates.contextSummary: Turek recapitulates six explanatory domains, argues atheism requires unsupported faith in unguided origins, and claims Silverman offered complaints rather than a rival explanation.

candidates.speaker: David Silverman
candidates.proposition: Theistic explanations have not demonstrated how reality works; honest atheism accepts uncertainty, relative morality, and human responsibility without inventing God.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator gives Silverman the final uninterrupted closing, whose first-person argument continues through his concluding thanks.
candidates.loadBearingReason: Silverman's closing answers the full theistic case, characterizes God as an unsupported gap-filler, and locates moral authority and responsibility in human choice.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Turek's closing claim that atheism explains none of the central features of reality and must borrow truth, reason, morality, and science from theism.

candidates.contextSummary: Silverman defends uncertainty about cosmic origins, reaffirms moral relativism, criticizes biblical morality, urges independent reading, and assigns humans responsibility for choosing right and wrong.
